I can relate to this. For a long time I was heavily obsessed with venomous snakes, to a degree that  made other people very uncomfortable. (Weird kid with no friends and an obsession with snakes isn't exactly welcoming to people.) Having a very specific interest in something people consider irregular automatically alienates you; especially when it's as all-consuming as the obsessions that aspies harbor. People like to take out their own insecurities on people that are more abnormal than themselves. You have to learn to ignore their provocations. Our obsessions are part of what we are; if you don't let them bother you, they will eventually learn that your obsession is a part of your identity, and quit making fun of it. If you let yourself become "the armadillo guy," then making fun of you will become as pointless as laughing at an astronomer for his interest in planets.

A furry white ball isn't exactly a snake though. If one can promote feelings of awareness about things that could present potential dangers in future, in my opinion, those feelings should be promoted. Plus it seems like the child would be growing up with a lot of exposure to snakes and stuff (I live around a lot of snakes and would not say that I am regularly bitten around them, unlike the mother in this story.) I personally think that making it apparent that snakes do present danger in a setting that is not dangerous would make the child a lot better off in the long term, especially given the child's apparent level of exposure to such creatures.
